transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor... I, uh, I didn't really want to come in today, to be honest with you. But it's just... it's gotten to be too much. I live over in this apartment complex—it's one of those older ones, you know, with the open walkways where you can see everybody walking by your front window. I've always just minded my own business, never bothered a soul, just kept to myself since I haven't been working. But... well, I came in because I know the people at my apartment are watching my comings and goings. 

Every single time I open my door, even if I'm just going to take the trash out to the dumpster out back, or walking down to check the mail, I can feel them tracking me. They peek out their blinds. And it's not just watching, they're... they're slipping notes about me to the office. I know they are. I see the papers being passed around. 

I've tried bringing it up, you know, trying to get it to stop, but everybody keeps telling me it's just notices on the doors. The manager, my family... they all just brush me off and say, "Oh, it's just a water shut-off notice, it's just a pest control flyer, everybody gets them." But I'm not a fool. I see the way they look at me when I walk past. You don't just put up that many papers unless you're tracking somebody, you know? They're keeping tabs on me and reporting back to the leasing office, and I just... I can't get a moment's peace in my own home with all this monitoring going on. It's exhausting, and nobody will listen to what's actually happening.
Have you ever seen, heard, or felt things that others don't seem to notice, like voices, visions, or sensations?

Voices? No, doctor, no... I don't have anything like that going on. I mean, I hear things, sure, but it's just the regular noises, you know? Like I was saying about that apartment building, it was built back in the seventies, I think, so the walls are just paper thin and they didn't put any good insulation in. I can hear the plumbing rattling when the guy upstairs takes a shower at two in the morning, and I hear the heavy footsteps on the concrete walkway outside—thump, thump, thump—every time one of them is walking past my window to keep an eye on me. 

I hear them muttering out there sometimes, too, but that's just them talking to each other, probably coordinating with the office. It's not... not imaginary voices in my head or anything like you see on those television programs. I don't see visions or ghosts or anything strange like that. My eyesight is perfectly fine for a man my age—well, I have to use those little reading glasses you buy at the pharmacy if I'm looking at the mail, but otherwise I see exactly what's actually out there in the real world. 

And I definitely don't feel things touching me or crawling on me when nobody's there. I just feel tired, honestly. Tired of the real people doing what they're doing. So, no, I don't hear or see things that aren't there. Everything I'm seeing and hearing is 100 percent real, right outside my front door.

Have there ever been times when you experienced things like strange beliefs that others don’t understand, hearing voices that others can’t hear, or acting in a very unusual or confused way that people around you found difficult to understand?

Well, strange beliefs... like I said, I know what I know about the apartment. People say they don't understand it, but that's just because they aren't the ones living it, you know? And I already told you I don't hear any imaginary voices. But... acting in a confused way? People not understanding what I'm doing? I guess... well, there was this one time recently. 

I used to go down to the senior center sometimes, just to get out of the apartment, away from the windows for a bit. They have this little workshop area in the back where they fix things up for the center, and I thought, you know, maybe I could help out. Keep my hands busy. They had this old wooden shelf that needed fixing—the brackets were all loose, and it was wobbling every time someone put a book on it. So I went over there to fix it. 

But I got there, and they had all these screws just dumped in a plastic bin. Big ones, little ones, Phillips head, flathead... just a big jumbled mess. And I don't know, I just... I couldn't start on the shelf until the screws were right. So I started taking them out, one by one, and lining them up on the workbench. I had to put the longest ones on the left, and then the next size down, all the way to the tiny little ones on the right. And they had to be perfectly straight. If one rolled a little bit, I had to fix it. And while I was doing it, I just kept tapping my knuckles on the table—tap, tap, tap—just to keep the rhythm, I guess. It felt like if I stopped tapping, the whole line of screws would be wrong. 

I must have been doing it for a long time, because this lady who runs the activities, she came over. She said, "Are you going to fix that shelf, or do you want to come sit down and have some coffee?" And I heard her, I really did, but... I couldn't move. I just stood there, staring at the screws, holding this yellow-handled screwdriver in my right hand. I couldn't put it down, and I couldn't go sit down, and I couldn't fix the shelf either. It was like my brain was a car stuck in neutral, just revving and revving but not going anywhere. I couldn't switch gears. I just stood there holding the tool, frozen, while she kept asking if I was alright. She looked at me like I was crazy, like she couldn't understand why I wouldn't just answer her or move. I think she ended up calling someone to come get me, because I just couldn't snap out of it. It was very... very confusing for everybody, I suppose.
Can you tell me more about what you believe the people in your apartment complex are doing exactly, and how long you’ve felt this way?

Well, exactly what they're doing... it's a whole system, doctor. It's not just one person acting alone, it's a coordinated effort. You see, they sit by their windows all day. Like the older woman down in apartment 2B, she has those cheap aluminum blinds, the ones that come standard with the place, and I know for a fact she bends the third slat down just a fraction of an inch. Just enough so she can peer out the second she hears my deadbolt unlatch. And she's writing it down—the exact time, what direction I'm walking, whether I have a grocery bag in my hand. 

Then the maintenance man, the fella who always wears that faded blue baseball cap, he makes his rounds on the walkway. He walks by, and she slips her little notes to him, or maybe leaves them under the edge of her welcome mat, and he gathers them all up and takes them straight to the leasing office. They are compiling a massive file on me, keeping a minute-by-minute log of my entire life. I don't know if they're trying to build a case to evict me or if someone is paying them to do it, but they are documenting everything. Every time I leave, every time I come back. 

And as for how long... well, I've spent a lot of time sitting in my chair in the dark trying to trace it all back to the exact beginning. Because it wasn't always like this, you know. When I first moved in, people just minded their own business. But... well, the suspicious thoughts about the apartment neighbors and office have been with me for about a year and a month. 

Yes, a year and a month exactly. I remember because it was right around the time they came through to do the mandatory air filter changes last fall. The maintenance guy came inside my place, and he was just lingering, you know? Looking around my living room a little too long, taking mental notes of where my things were, where I sit. And ever since that specific day, a year and a month ago, the whole atmosphere just shifted. That's when all those fake notices started appearing on the doors, and the blinds started snapping shut when I'd walk past. Thirteen months of this constant, exhausting surveillance. It's a very long time to live like a bug under a microscope, doctor, I'll tell you that much. You just can't relax for a single second.
Do you ever doubt that the people in your apartment are keeping detailed records of your activities, or do you feel completely certain that this is happening?

Doubt it? No. No, doctor, I don't have a single shred of doubt in my mind. I am completely, one hundred percent certain. In fact, that's... well, that's exactly why I came in here to talk to somebody, because I know—I absolutely *know*—the people at my apartment are watching my comings and goings. Every time I open my door, every time I step out onto that concrete walkway, they are tracking it, and they are slipping notes about me to the office. 

But the most frustrating part, the part that just makes me want to pull my hair out, is that everybody keeps telling me it's just notices on the doors. My sister, for instance, she came over a few weeks back, and she looked at one of the papers they taped up near my door. They always use that cheap blue painter's tape, you know, the kind that doesn't peel the paint off the cheap doors they installed. And she tells me, "Oh, it's just the management company putting out reminders about the dumpster rules," or "It's just the schedule for the pest control guy, why are you getting so worked up?" 

But she doesn't see the whole picture. She doesn't live there day in and day out. She doesn't sit there and watch the maintenance man fold up the real notes—the handwritten notes from the woman in 2B about exactly what time I left to get milk, or how long I stood outside checking my mailbox—and tuck them right in with those fake printed notices. They hide it right out in the open! So everyone else just walks by, they see a piece of paper taped to a door, and they think it's perfectly normal apartment business. They just refuse to open their eyes. But I know what I see. I know they are slipping those notes about me to the office, no matter how many times people try to convince me it's just regular maintenance flyers. I know the truth of it.
